classification.difficultyReason: Generate members satisfying familiar verbal rules, respect numerical bounds and record distinct elements in set notation; prime identification is the hardest direct application.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess conversion from a verbal set description to an element listing. Pages 2–3 establish that set method. They do not establish the prerequisite methods for generating odd numbers, multiples, perfect squares or primes.
questions.methodNote: List every distinct element, separate elements with commas and enclose the list in curly brackets. Order is immaterial and repeated elements count once.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List elements satisfying familiar descriptions and write them using set notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate three explicitly listed sets into concise verbal descriptions.

questions.mappingNote: Each part reverses the taught description-to-list relationship. Part a identifies consecutive alphabet letters; part b identifies odd whole numbers; part c identifies the first four primes. Set notation is the directly assessed skill. Earlier teaching of prime numbers is not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Describe a listed set by a clear property identifying exactly its elements. Page 2 demonstrates equivalent listed and verbal descriptions and explains that sets must be well-defined.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate three explicitly listed sets into concise verbal descriptions.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the ambiguity criterion, distinguishing subjective descriptions from fixed membership and noticing the unspecified election or time in voting membership.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks whether the membership rule is unambiguous. Parts a, d and e use subjective descriptions; b and c have objective rules; f fixes the present time and room; g omits the election or time needed to fix voting membership.
questions.methodNote: A set is well-defined when its elements can be described or listed clearly and without ambiguity; page 2 contrasts ‘tall people’ with letters in the English alphabet, and page 3 repeats the criterion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the definition of a well-defined set to familiar descriptions and explain ambiguous membership.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare explicitly listed or simply described sets, ignoring element order and repetition.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the equal-set definition on page 2, reinforced by the summary on page 3. Part c also evaluates the supplied addition.
questions.methodNote: Sets are equal when they contain exactly the same elements. Element order does not matter, and repeated elements count once.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare explicitly listed or simply described sets, ignoring element order and repetition.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare the elements of two sets, ignoring order and repetition.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts directly assess equality of sets using the definitions and examples on page 2 and the summary on page 3.
questions.methodNote: Equal sets have exactly the same elements. Element order does not matter, and repetitions are counted once.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare the elements of two sets, ignoring order and repetition.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate explicit element-membership sentences directly into symbols.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly apply the membership notation taught on page 3; no additional numerical method is needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines elements of a set. Page 3 explicitly translates ‘is an element of’ into ∈ and ‘is not an element of’ into ∉, with numerical examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate explicit element-membership sentences directly into symbols.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise membership of explicitly listed or verbally described sets.

questions.mappingNote: Every part asks for membership notation, so set-notation-fundamentals is the directly assessed skill. Original prerequisite teaching for perfect squares and prime numbers is absent; compatibility for parts f–g remains unverified.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 defines membership and non-membership using ∈ and ∉. Page 2 explains listed and verbally described sets; page 4 lists even whole numbers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise membership of explicitly listed or verbally described sets.

classification.difficultyReason: First decide whether membership is determinate, then distinguish finite collections from infinite ones, recognising that bounded fractions remain infinite while an enormous bounded integer set is finite.

questions.mappingNote: Each part applies these definitions directly: a has an ambiguous adjective; b, d and f describe bounded real-world collections; c and e have endlessly many members; g has fixed whole-number bounds. Set notation fundamentals is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 require an unambiguous membership rule. Pages 4–5 distinguish finite collections whose elements can all be listed from infinite collections that always have further elements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply well-definedness and finite/infinite definitions to familiar mathematical and everyday collections.

classification.difficultyReason: Count distinct elements, including empty sets and repeated entries.

questions.mappingNote: Set cardinality is the directly assessed skill; primes and squares supply elements in f and g.
questions.methodNote: Count distinct elements; repetitions count once. Page 5 defines set size, singleton sets and the empty set. Earlier prerequisite teaching for generating primes and squares is absent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count distinct elements, including empty sets and repeated entries.

classification.difficultyReason: Generate elements from each rule, choose terminating or continuing notation and classify finiteness; multiples above 50 require finding the first valid member before continuing the pattern.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses set listing and finite/infinite classification.
questions.methodNote: Use curly brackets and commas; use ellipses for clear patterns. A finite list ends, whereas an infinite set always has further elements. Earlier prerequisite generation methods for b, c, e, f and g are not supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List set elements and distinguish terminating lists from unlimited patterns.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine whether a described set contains any elements.

questions.mappingNote: Direct application of empty-set notation and meaning.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 defines the empty set as having no elements. Establish non-emptiness by giving an element.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine whether a described set contains any elements.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain claims about finiteness, equality and cardinality, using a counterexample where needed.

questions.mappingNote: Set fundamentals governs the claims; e additionally uses a counterexample.
questions.methodNote: Use equality as identical membership, finiteness as a terminating complete list, and the uniqueness of the empty set. Disprove the converse cardinality claim with two unequal sets of equal size.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain claims about finiteness, equality and cardinality, using a counterexample where needed.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish equality of sets from equality of cardinalities, count distinct members and apply the zero-element, singleton and repetition rules.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b distinguish equal sizes from equal sets; c–d use the equality rules on page 2; e–g count elements using page 5; h–j apply singleton, repetition and empty-set rules. Original prerequisite instruction for identifying primes and generating multiples is absent for e–f.
questions.methodNote: Compare actual elements for set equality; ignore order and repeated entries. For cardinality, count distinct elements. A singleton has size one and the empty set has size zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare sets and their cardinalities, accounting for order, repeated elements, singleton sets and the empty set.

classification.difficultyReason: Check whether every member of the first category belongs to the second, using exceptions such as the even prime 2 to reject inclusion.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess subset notation. Part c additionally requires recognising 2 as a prime that is not odd; original prerequisite teaching evidence for prime numbers was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition that every element of a subset belongs to the other set. A single element outside the other set establishes that it is not a subset. Page 8 connects these relations to 'all' and 'not all'.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select subset notation using familiar categories and one numerical counterexample.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare membership in the supplied sets, identify a counterexample when inclusion fails and apply the taught empty-set and self-subset rules.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e and k compare listed elements; f–i apply the empty-set and self-subset rules. Part j additionally requires recognising that 9 is not prime; original prerequisite teaching evidence is missing.
questions.methodNote: Check whether every element of the first set belongs to the second. One element outside the second set establishes non-inclusion. The empty set and the set itself are always subsets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the definition of a subset, including empty sets and the set itself.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain subset properties using element membership, equality and finite cardinality.

questions.mappingNote: All seven parts directly assess explanations of subset notation and its consequences. No prerequisite prime, multiple or square-number methods are required.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of subset: every element of the first set belongs to the second. Page 7 explains self-subsets and the empty set; page 5 defines cardinality and singleton sets; page 8 reinforces the all-elements interpretation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain subset properties using element membership, equality and finite cardinality.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct counterexamples to universal claims by separating containment from cardinality, then justify a cardinality inequality through successive subset relations.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the self-subset rule; part b distinguishes failed containment from element counts; part c uses equality of sets; part d applies successive containment to compare finite cardinalities.
questions.methodNote: Use cardinality as the number of elements, the definition of a subset, and the fact that a set is a subset of itself. Explain true statements through element containment and disprove false statements with finite examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing subset relationships from cardinality relationships and explaining false statements with counterexamples.

classification.difficultyReason: Enumerate all subsets systematically and identify the pattern in their counts.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses subset notation, complete enumeration and subset counts; set-notation-fundamentals is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a subset, including the empty set and the set itself. Enumerate subsets by cardinality, count them, and identify the powers-of-two pattern.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Enumerate all subsets systematically and identify the pattern in their counts.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the two categories and translate the supplied 'all' or 'not all' wording into the corresponding directed subset relation.

questions.mappingNote: Each part describes two sets and translates the supplied universal or non-universal statement into the corresponding relation. Parts b and d use numerical set descriptions; earlier prerequisite teaching about even numbers and multiples was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines subset and not-subset through element membership. Page 8 explicitly translates ‘all’ into subset notation and ‘not all’ into not-subset notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate statements using ‘all’ and ‘not all’ into subset notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct examples satisfying three simultaneous subset conditions, including a failed subset relation.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts construct explicit finite sets and verify the requested subset relations using the definitions on pages 7–8. No prime, multiple or other prerequisite generation method is required.
questions.methodNote: A subset contains only elements belonging to the containing set. To establish that one set is not a subset of another, identify an element belonging to the first but not the second.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct examples satisfying three simultaneous subset conditions, including a failed subset relation.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct examples satisfying two simultaneous subset conditions.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts construct sets using the subset and non-subset definitions on page 7 and their all/not-all interpretation on page 8; page 5 supports finite-set notation.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a subset: every element must belong to the other set. Establish a non-subset relationship by exhibiting an element outside the other set.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct examples satisfying two simultaneous subset conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: Read filled-dot positions on explicitly labelled number lines and write those values as sets, including a singleton.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts reverse the page-10 demonstration of the set {0,1,4}; pages 2–3 establish set notation.
questions.methodNote: Read the values marked by filled dots and list them between curly brackets, separated by commas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read marked whole numbers and list the elements using set notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate distance from 6 into a two-sided strict interval, filter for even whole numbers and plot the survivors; also recognise an empty set after combining interval and parity restrictions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e directly use the demonstrated set-to-number-line method. Parts f–l also require prerequisite parity, primes, distance, endpoint or mixed-number interpretation; original prerequisite teaching evidence is missing.
questions.methodNote: Represent each set member by a filled dot at its whole-number value. Page 5 establishes the empty set.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret membership conditions, distances and mixed-number bounds, then represent each set.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine subset membership, cardinality and a maximum-element condition.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 supplies whole-number membership, page 5 defines |A|, page 7 defines subsets, and page 2 defines listing distinct set elements.
questions.methodNote: Whole numbers begin at zero; subset notation restricts membership and cardinality counts distinct elements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine subset membership, cardinality and a maximum-element condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine each pair of supplied membership descriptions using 'and' for intersection and inclusive 'or' for union, as explicitly requested.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts directly apply these verbal definitions to the supplied sets. Parts c and d also use prior geometry and number vocabulary whose original prerequisite teaching is not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Pages 11–12 define intersection as membership in both sets and union as membership in either set, and explicitly associate these with and and inclusive or.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate intersection and union notation into descriptions using and and or.

classification.difficultyReason: Describe intersections and unions of contextual sets and decide whether their memberships overlap.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 directly applies the contextual intersection examples on page 11 and the inclusive-or and disjoint-set definitions on page 12. Page 5 supplies empty-set notation; pages 7–8 supply set membership and subset context. Page 10 is background only.
questions.methodNote: Use intersection for elements belonging to both sets, union for elements belonging to either set with inclusive ‘or’, and an empty intersection to identify disjoint sets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Describe intersections and unions of contextual sets and decide whether their memberships overlap.

classification.difficultyReason: Find shared members and combine distinct members, interpreting ellipses as consecutive ranges, then use whether the intersection is empty to decide disjointness.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly apply the finite-set intersection and union examples on pages 11–12 and the empty-intersection criterion on page 12. Part e also uses the whole-number and ellipsis conventions illustrated on pages 5 and 10. No prime-generation or square-generation method is required because every element is supplied.
questions.methodNote: Intersection lists elements belonging to both sets; union lists elements belonging to either set without repetition. Sets are disjoint exactly when their intersection is empty.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly identify common elements, combine distinct elements and test whether the intersection is empty.

classification.difficultyReason: Enumerate verbally described sets, compute their intersection and union, then transfer each result to a separate number-line representation.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly combines the taught set operations and number-line representation. Part b first enumerates the two described sets, then applies those same methods. Earlier teaching for generating odd numbers is not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use common elements for intersection and all elements without repetitions for union. Page 10 defines whole numbers starting at zero and represents finite sets with closed dots on labelled number lines; pages 11–12 teach intersection and union.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find intersections and unions, interpret verbal set descriptions, and represent each result on a number line.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply intersection successively across three supplied sets, distinguishing membership in all three from pairwise overlap, and form a union without repetition.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess intersection and union of three explicitly listed finite sets; set-notation-fundamentals is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 11–12 define intersection as common membership and union as membership in either set. Apply these definitions successively to three sets, listing each union element once. Page 5 establishes empty-set notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find common elements and combine explicitly listed elements across three finite sets.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct suitable subsets and coordinate subsequent choices so that the subsets are disjoint, including infinite subsets.

questions.mappingNote: All four responses construct subsets; the second response in each group depends on the first. Set-notation fundamentals directly covers subsets, infinite sets and disjointness.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a subset, the endless nature of infinite sets, whole numbers beginning at zero, and the definition of disjoint sets as sets with no common elements. Page 12 explicitly illustrates disjoint even and odd sets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct suitable subsets and coordinate subsequent choices so that the subsets are disjoint, including infinite subsets.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain general subset relationships using the definitions of intersection, union and the empty set.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply the intersection definition; c applies the inclusive union definition; d combines these definitions; e and f apply the empty-subset property explicitly taught on page 7 and summarised on page 8. No earlier prerequisite method is needed.
questions.methodNote: Use membership definitions: an intersection contains elements in both sets, a union contains elements in either or both sets, and a subset has every element in the containing set. The empty set is a subset of every set because it has no element outside that set.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain general subset relationships using the definitions of intersection, union and the empty set.

classification.difficultyReason: Reason with arbitrary sets to simplify union and intersection, connecting subset containment to which set remains and applying empty-set and self-operation definitions.

questions.mappingNote: All six completions directly assess elementary set identities using the definitions taught on these pages.
questions.methodNote: Use the empty-set definition, subset membership, union as elements in either set and intersection as elements in both sets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the definitions of subset, union, intersection and the empty set to complete six identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Justify general set-cardinality statements and disprove false statements using finite counterexamples.

questions.mappingNote: Each part tests a universal statement about finite sets. Parts a–b use the empty-set identities; parts c–d require counterexamples. The counterexamples skill is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the number-of-elements notation and the empty-set definition on page 5, and the union/intersection definitions and finite listed-set examples on pages 11–12. Establish true statements from these definitions; disprove false statements by listing a finite counterexample and counting its elements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Justify general set-cardinality statements and disprove false statements using finite counterexamples.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the elements excluded from a named set within its given universal set.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the complement definition to a verbal description of S and E. Set notation is the primary assessed skill; no Venn diagram construction or counting rule is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 defines the complement of S as all elements of the given universal set E that are not in S; page 15 reiterates this definition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the elements excluded from a named set within its given universal set.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a supplied Venn diagram and combine complements, unions and intersections.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses set operations and complement notation using a supplied single-set Venn diagram. Pages 7–8 establish subsets and E; pages 11–12 establish intersection and union; pages 14–15 establish complements and Venn regions.
questions.methodNote: Read elements from their regions in the universal rectangle. Complement means elements of E outside the set; intersection means common elements; union includes elements in either set.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret a supplied Venn diagram and combine complements, unions and intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain complement identities and disprove a cardinality claim using a counterexample.

questions.mappingNote: Each part tests set notation and complement reasoning directly. Part f also requires comparing cardinalities and supplying a counterexample.
questions.methodNote: Interpret a complement as elements of the universal set not in the given set; use union, intersection and the empty set to explain identities. Disprove a general statement with an explicit counterexample.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain complement identities and disprove a cardinality claim using a counterexample.

classification.difficultyReason: Read elements directly from labelled Venn regions, including intersection, union and set differences.

questions.mappingNote: All seven parts directly apply the source's region-based interpretation of set notation; no counting or inclusion–exclusion calculation is required.
questions.methodNote: Read the universal set from the rectangle, each set from its circle, the intersection from the overlap and the union from both circles. For 'not in', exclude the other circle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read elements directly from labelled Venn regions, including intersection, union and set differences.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret overlapping Venn regions and combine complements with unions and intersections.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts apply source-taught set notation directly to the supplied overlapping-set diagram. Compound expressions use the same region selection method without introducing additional algebraic laws.
questions.methodNote: Read membership from circles within universal rectangle E. Intersection means both, union means either or both, and complement means elements of E outside the named set or combined region.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret overlapping Venn regions and combine complements with unions and intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate each stated relationship into a taught circle arrangement, preserving subset direction and showing overlap without containment when neither set is a subset.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 directly assesses construction of Venn diagrams from set relationships; pages 7–8 teach subset containment, page 11 illustrates overlapping sets, and page 12 defines and illustrates disjoint sets.
questions.methodNote: Use a rectangle for the universal set, nested circles for subsets, separate circles for disjoint sets, and overlapping circles for sets with common elements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent directly stated subset, disjoint and overlapping relationships using two-set Venn diagrams.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct disjoint, overlapping and nested Venn diagrams from listed sets, then identify their unions and intersections.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 directly assesses constructing Venn diagrams for listed sets; union and intersection notation supports the diagram construction. Page 15 explicitly teaches overlapping, disjoint and nested representations; pages 7–8 teach subsets and pages 11–12 define union, intersection and disjoint sets.
questions.methodNote: Place common elements in overlapping regions and remaining elements in their respective circles. Draw disjoint circles for sets with no common elements and nested circles for a subset. List the union from either circle and the intersection from their common region.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct disjoint, overlapping and nested Venn diagrams from listed sets, then identify their unions and intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Sort the listed elements into common, exclusive and outside regions, record counts rather than elements, and read union and intersection totals from the requested diagram.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses constructing and interpreting region-count Venn diagrams from listed sets, followed by union and intersection cardinalities.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 distinguishes elements from bracketed region counts and counts the overlap once. Examples 1 and 2 on pages 17–18 fill the intersection, the two exclusive regions and the outside region. Page 19 states the inclusion–exclusion rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two-set Venn diagrams from explicitly listed sets, count each region and state the union and intersection cardinalities.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate six contexts into overlapping sets, identify the union or intersection and calculate intersection or outside-region counts.

questions.mappingNote: Part a identifies sum 7 as the intersection and uses all 100 rolls as the union. Part b uses the stated all-play condition as the union. Part c identifies the three coin amounts as the intersection and uses all 100 girls as the union. Parts d and e calculate the union then subtract it from 100 to obtain neither. Part f uses the all-play condition to recover the intersection. The directly assessed skill is two-set inclusion–exclusion.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 introduces counts in the four regions, places counts in round brackets and explains subtracting the overlap once. Examples 1 and 2 on pages 17–18 fill the intersection, exclusive regions and outside region. Page 19 states the two-set inclusion–exclusion formula. Apply these methods to the six word problems, drawing the requested Venn diagrams for a–e.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate six contexts into overlapping sets, identify the union or intersection and calculate intersection or outside-region counts.

classification.difficultyReason: Build the exclusive regions from the supplied overlap, combine them with the overlap for either item, then subtract that union from the group total to find neither.

questions.mappingNote: The four-region construction and neither count follow Example 3 on page 20.
questions.methodNote: Fill the overlap first, calculate the two exclusive regions and subtract their union from the universal total.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine all four regions from two totals, their overlap and the universal total.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent walking and swimming as overlapping sets, derive each exclusive count, interpret 'or' inclusively, and subtract the union from all animals to obtain neither.

questions.mappingNote: Example 3 supplies the same overlap-first contextual counting method; the source's a/b then c/d two-column order is retained.
questions.methodNote: Construct the four disjoint regions and obtain each requested count from them.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use a given intersection to calculate exclusive, union and outside counts.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover an unknown intersection from inclusive totals before calculating the other regions.

questions.mappingNote: Example 2 on page 18 explicitly recovers an intersection from a union; Example 3 on page 20 supports contextual interpretation.
questions.methodNote: Use the excess of the summed set totals over the union to find the overlap, then complete the four-region Venn diagram.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover an unknown intersection from inclusive totals before calculating the other regions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that everyone belongs to the union, recover the overlap and combine the exclusive regions.

questions.mappingNote: Page 18 Example 2 teaches recovering the overlap from a union; page 20 Example 3 teaches exactly-one counts.
questions.methodNote: Identify the universal total as the union, recover the overlap and add the two exclusive regions for exactly one activity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that everyone belongs to the union, recover the overlap and combine the exclusive regions.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish neither, exactly one and at least one failure using the regions of two overlapping sets.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 applies the same two-set counting method to pass/fail outcomes. Exactly one pass and exactly one failure select the same two exclusive regions; at least one failure excludes only the intersection.
questions.methodNote: Identify the two sets, enter the intersection first, subtract it from each set total to obtain the exclusive regions, and subtract all three internal regions from the universal total. Example 3 on page 20 demonstrates this method; page 21 instructs students to solve each Exercise 23H problem by drawing a Venn diagram.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish neither, exactly one and at least one failure using the regions of two overlapping sets.
